---
title: "Desktop App Architecture"
number-sections: true
---

This page is for developers. It explains how the DigiQual app is put together, how the Windows and macOS installers are built, and why it's built this way. To *use* the app, see [Launch the App](gui.qmd).

## The Short Version {#sec-short-version}

- **All of the app's code lives in the `digiqual` package**, in the `digiqual.gui` subpackage. It ships inside the normal `digiqual` wheel on PyPI, so `pip install digiqual` always includes the app.
- **The desktop installers are that same wheel**, installed into a self-contained Python by [Briefcase](https://briefcase.beeware.org/). The top-level `app/` folder holds only Briefcase's configuration and a two-line entry point; there's no app code in it.

So any change to the app goes into `src/digiqual/gui/`, and every way of launching the app picks it up.

## Where Everything Lives {#sec-layout}

```text
src/digiqual/
├── gui/                        ← the app (a normal subpackage of digiqual)
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── __main__.py             ← makes `python -m digiqual.gui` work
│   ├── app.py                  ← the page shell (header, stepper, hidden navset of stages) + server()
│   ├── components.py           ← STAGES (order and names), the stage page template, shared helpers
│   ├── state.py                ← per-session shared state, invalidation and the explorer settings
│   ├── stepper.py              ← the workflow stepper: status rules (pure function) and rendering
│   ├── start_page.py           ← the start page (entry cards and stage overview)
│   ├── about_page.py           ← the About page (version, links, papers, funders)
│   ├── stage_design.py         ← 1. Simulation Design (UI + server logic)
│   ├── stage_data.py           ← 2. Data Diagnostics
│   ├── stage_model.py          ← 3. Model Diagnostics (Run models: background fit with progress)
│   ├── stage_explorer.py       ← 4. Model Explorer
│   ├── stage_pod.py            ← 5. PoD Analysis
│   ├── background.py           ← runs slow steps in a worker thread; progress tracking and panel
│   ├── launcher.py             ← starts the server and opens the window (with its Help menu)
│   └── www/                    ← static files served by Shiny: app.css, favicon.png, the funder
│                                 logos and, if downloaded, mathjax-tex-svg.js
├── _digiqual_cpp.*.so / .pyd   ← compiled C++ extension (built by setup.py)
└── ...                         ← the statistical library itself

app/                            ← Briefcase wrapper only (not part of the wheel)
├── pyproject.toml              ← [tool.briefcase] config: name, version, icon, platform options
├── .python-version             ← Python used for desktop builds (3.12)
├── src/digiqual_desktop/
│   └── __main__.py             ← entry point: sets sys.frozen, calls launcher.main()
├── icons/                      ← app icons (.icns / .ico / .png), generated
└── *.csv                       ← example datasets for trying the app

scripts/make_icon.py            ← draws the icon; writes app/icons/, gui/www/favicon.png, docs/www/
.github/workflows/build_app.yml ← builds, self-tests and packages the installers
```

The static files in `gui/www/` are included in the wheel by `package_data` in `setup.py` and `MANIFEST.in`. `app.py` finds them relative to its own location, so this works the same installed or from a checkout.

MathJax (which renders the model equation) is not kept in the repository. `mathjax-tex-svg.js` is downloaded into `www/` at build time, by `just fetch_mathjax` or the `build_app.yml` workflow, so the desktop app works offline. Without it, `app.py` loads MathJax from a CDN instead.

## How Results Flow Between Stages {#sec-state}

Each stage's results depend on the stages before it. `state.py` holds the per-session `AppState`, and `register_shared()` keeps the study in sync with the data: a new file or column choice builds a new `SimulationStudy` and calls `AppState.invalidate("data")`, which clears every result. `invalidate("diagnostics")` clears only the diagnostics (the model doesn't use them).

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    D[Data + columns<br/>study_instance] --> G[Diagnostics<br/>diagnostic_table]
    G -. unlocks .-> C[Candidate models<br/>candidates_ready]
    D --> C
    C --> M[Chosen model<br/>model_fit]
    M --> E[Explorer settings<br/>explorer_config]
    E --> A[Applied PoD setup<br/>applied_structure]
    A --> U[Bootstrap<br/>uq_result]
```

- New data or columns clear everything. Changing a diagnostic threshold only marks the diagnostics as out of date (`diagnostics_stale`).
- The candidate models are cross-validated once per dataset, when the user presses Run models in Model Diagnostics (which needs the diagnostics to have run). `candidates_ready` is then set, and `model_fit` holds the `study.fit_model()` result for the chosen model.
- `explorer_config` (a `reactive.calc`) is the single source of the model, the plotted, integrated and sliced variables and the threshold. `AppState.structure(config)` is the part that needs the Update PoD button (model, plotted and integrated variables, distributions and ranges); after Update PoD it is stored as `applied_structure`. When the current structure differs from it, the explorer asks for Update PoD and the PoD Analysis stage won't run. Slices and the threshold are not part of it: they update the plots live. Choosing another model therefore needs Update PoD, like a role change, and marks the bootstrap out of date.
- The bootstrap result (`uq_result`) is a record of everything the run used: `config` (the explorer settings), `fit` (model metrics, equation, name and dropdown choice), `settings` (iterations, `n_jobs`, target PoD and confidence, CSV name, columns and diagnostic thresholds), `results` (the `pod()` output) and `spectrum` (the threshold spectrum, for one plotted variable). When `config` no longer matches `explorer_config`, the PoD Analysis stage marks the result as out of date instead of discarding it. The exports are built from this record.

### From app settings to library calls {#sec-analysis-kwargs}

`state.analysis_kwargs(study, config)` is the single translation from an explorer config to `study.pod()` arguments: `poi_col`, `nuisance_col`, `slice_values`, `nuisance_dists`, `nuisance_bounds`, and `model_override` / `force_degree` from the config's model key (via `core.model_key_args`). `AppState.pod_kwargs()` is a thin wrapper around it. Two other module-level helpers go with it: `nuisance_dists_for()` fits the chosen distributions (one that can't be fitted is left out, so that variable is integrated uniformly) and `column_values()` gives a column's numeric values. Update PoD, the live updates and the bootstrap all use it.

### Background tasks {#sec-background}

The three slow steps (Run models or a model change, Update PoD, the bootstrap) run in a worker thread as `reactive.extended_task`s, so the page stays live. While a task runs, `fit_running` / `pod_running` / `uq_running` in `AppState` are set, the stepper shows a spinner, and the explorer's live updates pause so nothing else changes the study. `background.py` provides the pieces:

- `TaskProgress` follows one task: the library's log messages from its thread (which mark its steps) and its `(done, total, label)` progress callback (`fit_model` and `pod` take one).
- `step_states(reached, n)` turns "how far it got" into each step's state (`done`, `active`, `todo`).
- `progress_panel()` draws the panel once: spinner, elapsed time, bar and steps.
- `push_progress()` then updates it in place twice a second through a custom message, handled in the browser by `PROGRESS_JS` (added to the page head in `app.py`). Redrawing the panel instead would restart its spinners.

## Ways the App Gets Launched {#sec-launch-modes}

Every route ends up in the same function, `digiqual.gui.launcher.main()`:

| How it's started | Path to `launcher.main()` |
|---|---|
| Desktop app (MSI / zip / DMG) | Briefcase's executable → `digiqual_desktop/__main__.py` → `main()` |
| `digiqual` command (`uv tool install`, `uvx digiqual`) | `[project.gui-scripts]` in `pyproject.toml` → `main()` |
| `dq_ui()` in Python / Jupyter | starts `python -m digiqual.gui` in a new process → `main()` |
| `python -m digiqual.gui` | `gui/__main__.py` → `main()` |
| `just app` (from a checkout) | `uv run python -m digiqual.gui` → `main()` |
| `just app_dev` | `shiny run digiqual.gui.app:app`: browser only, skips the launcher (for UI work) |

## What `launcher.main()` Does {#sec-launcher}

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[main] --> B{Started as a multiprocessing<br/>worker or resource tracker?}
    B -- yes --> C[Run that task, then exit]
    B -- no --> D[Set up logging to digiqual.log<br/>Point empty stdout/stderr at it]
    D --> E{--self-test?}
    E -- yes --> F[Check C++ extension, pywebview,<br/>worker processes and HTTP server<br/>Exit 0 or 1]
    E -- no --> G[Start the Shiny server on a free<br/>127.0.0.1 port, in a background thread]
    G --> H[Wait until it answers HTTP]
    H --> I[Open a pywebview window<br/>WebView2 on Windows, WebKit on macOS]
    I -- fails --> J[Fall back to an Edge app window on Windows,<br/>otherwise the default browser]
```

`launcher.py` keeps its module-level imports light (shiny and pywebview are only imported inside functions), because worker processes import it before they know they are workers.

## Why It's Built This Way {#sec-design-decisions}

These are the decisions most likely to puzzle someone reading the code, with the reason for each.

### Briefcase rather than PyInstaller {#sec-briefcase}

PyInstaller *freezes* an app: it analyses imports to decide which files to bundle. That missed Shiny's static files, pythonnet's DLLs and some hidden imports, which needed a long hand-maintained `.spec` file. Briefcase instead runs `pip install` into a bundled, standalone Python. The app therefore gets exactly the files a normal install would, including the prebuilt C++ extension from the `digiqual` wheel. Nothing has to be listed by hand.

### Worker processes and `sys.frozen` {#sec-worker-processes}

The PoD bootstrap runs in parallel with `joblib` (`backend="multiprocessing"`), which starts worker processes by running `sys.executable` again. In the desktop app, `sys.executable` is the DigiQual app itself, not `python`, and it can't run `python -c "..."` commands. Without special handling, every worker would open another DigiQual window.

To prevent this, `digiqual_desktop/__main__.py` sets `sys.frozen = True`. That makes Python's `multiprocessing` start workers as `DigiQual --multiprocessing-fork ...`. The first thing `launcher.main()` does is spot those arguments, and the `-c` commands used by Python's and joblib's resource trackers, and run the requested task instead of the app. This mirrors what PyInstaller's runtime hooks do.

### Redirecting stdout and stderr {#sec-stdio}

A desktop app has no console, so `sys.stdout` and `sys.stderr` are `None`. uvicorn, the web server under Shiny, calls `.isatty()` on them while setting up logging, and crashes the server thread. The window then shows a blank page. The launcher points them at the log file before starting the server.

### Build details in `build_app.yml` {#sec-build-details}

| Detail | Reason |
|---|---|
| Python **3.12** | pywebview's Windows backend needs pythonnet, which supports up to Python 3.13. |
| macOS **12.0** minimum (`min_os_version`) | scipy and scikit-learn only publish Apple Silicon wheels for macOS 12+. |
| The `digiqual` wheel is built in the job and passed to Briefcase with `-C requires=[...]` | PyPI has an identically named wheel, and pip may otherwise choose that one. The installers must contain the code being built. |
| A `proxy_tools` wheel is built in the job | pywebview needs `proxy_tools`, which is only published as source code. Briefcase installs wheels only, so without this pip silently falls back to the ancient pywebview 3.4, which has no menu support. `pywebview>=5.0` in `pyproject.toml` makes that fail loudly instead. |
| Self-test runs **without** redirected output | It behaves like a user double-clicking the app, so the stdout/stderr problem above would be caught. |

## The Build Pipeline {#sec-build-pipeline}

`.github/workflows/build_app.yml` runs on Windows and macOS:

1. Build the `digiqual` wheel for Python 3.12 with cibuildwheel. This is the same C++ build that goes to PyPI.
2. Build a `proxy_tools` wheel.
3. `briefcase create` and `briefcase build`: the standalone Python, the app executable, and every dependency installed from wheels.
4. Run `DigiQual --self-test`, which must exit 0.
5. `briefcase package`: an MSI and a portable zip on Windows, a DMG on macOS. Signing is ad hoc (no certificate) for now.
6. Upload them as run artifacts.

It runs in two situations:

- **Manually** (`just trigger_build`, or *Actions → Build App Executables → Run workflow*): this stops at the run artifacts, which you need to be logged in to GitHub to download.
- **On a version tag** (`vX.Y.Z`, pushed by `just patch` / `just minor`): an extra job creates the GitHub Release, if it doesn't exist yet, and attaches the installers. The [download instructions](gui.qmd) link to `/releases/latest`.

The version comes from `app/pyproject.toml`, which `just bump` keeps in step with the package version.

## Working on the App Locally {#sec-local-dev}

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Run the app in a browser, without the launcher (restart it to see code changes) | `just app_dev` |
| Run the full desktop window from your checkout | `just app` |
| Check the C++ extension, workers and server, without a window | `uv run python -m digiqual.gui --self-test` |
| Build the desktop app on your own machine | `uv tool install briefcase`, then `just build_app_local` |
| Build the installers in CI | `gh workflow run build_app.yml --ref <branch>` |
| Change the icon | Edit `scripts/make_icon.py`, then run `uv run python scripts/make_icon.py` |

`--self-test` results, and everything the app prints, go to the log file:

- **Windows:** `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Digiqual\digiqual.log`
- **macOS:** `~/Library/Logs/Digiqual/digiqual.log`
- **Linux:** `~/.local/share/Digiqual/digiqual.log`

## Common Changes {#sec-common-changes}

**Adding a dependency.** Add it to `dependencies` in the root `pyproject.toml`; the desktop app picks it up through the wheel. Check that it publishes wheels for Windows x64, macOS arm64 (macOS 12+) and Python 3.12. If it only publishes source, the desktop build fails or falls back to an older version; build a wheel of it in `build_app.yml` the way `proxy_tools` is.

**Adding a static file** (an image, CSS or JavaScript) to the app: put it in `src/digiqual/gui/www/` and refer to it by file name (e.g. `src="my_image.png"`). It is packaged automatically.

**Adding a page or feature to the app:** edit the relevant `stage_*.py` module. Each builds its page with `components.stage_page()` (settings sidebar, results, Back / Next) and has a `register(...)` function with its server logic; shared reactive state lives in `state.py`. A new stage is a new module, added to `STAGE_MODULES` in `app.py`, to `STAGES` in `components.py` (which names the stages everywhere: stepper, start page, buttons), to the status rules in `stepper.stage_statuses` and, if those rules need new state, to `snapshot()` in `stepper.register`. A page that is not a stage (like Start and About) is a `ui.nav_panel` added to the `navset_hidden` in `app.py` and to the `("start", "about")` check in `stepper_ui`, which hides the stepper on it. Navigation needs no server code per button: `components.nav_button()` sets the `goto_stage` input from the browser and one effect in `stepper.py` switches stage. Prefer calling library functions (and `digiqual.defaults` for default values) over re-implementing statistics in the GUI. Nothing in `app/` or the workflow needs to change.

**The desktop menu.** The native window has a **Help** menu with *View Documentation* (opens the docs site in the browser) and *About DigiQual* (the version). It is defined in `launcher.launch_webview_window`, so it only exists in the pywebview window, not in a browser.
